items.title: 67247_J.C. Higginbotham oral history interview
items.q: He came and told me, he said, 'I'm going to steal every thing that I can from you.' And I said, 'Thank you.'

ctx.x: You influenced like most of the trombone players since your time, I mean you've been like one of the major influences in jazz, I said and you have influenced so many young trombone players, I mean trombone players since your playing. What are some of the trombone players that you've listened to that you also we impressed by their playing ... or even younger ones.

I'd be glad to say it, Trummy Young. Note for note. He came and told me, he said, "I'm going to steal every thing that I can from you." And I said, "Thank you." It made me work harder. I have a record I made back there over in Denmark and the guy, I have his picture there, he sent for me. He owned a chocolate factory over there and he was a very nice guy. items.title: 52300_Trummy Young oral history interview
items.q: I only knew him when he got popular in later years. But I left Savannah in 1926.

ctx.x: Was there anyone else who came out of Savannah that stayed in music and made any kind of a name?

Later years but I didn't know him them. James Moody came out of Savannah. But I didn't know Moody at that particular time. I guess there are other guys who I really don't know who were musicians in Savannah that came out. There were good musicians all through the South, Atlanta and Savannah. Higginbotham came from Atlanta, J. C. did. He was originally -- he was born down in Georgia (inaudible). Quite a few good guys came from down around in that district, but I didn't know any of them back, there then. You know,…
